scope: Primary-source verification for rendering; dated snapshots, with no claim of exhaustive recency.

indicators.title: Americans' perceived control over AI in their lives
indicators.population: U.S. adults, Pew Research Center American Trends Panel wave 173; nationally representative weighted estimates.
indicators.question_description: Perceived amount of control over whether AI is used in one's life.

chart.title: Perceived control over whether AI is used in everyday life

data.label: A great deal / Quite a bit

chart.aggregation: These three groups and values are published by Pew, not estimated as complements.

source_figure.locator: First control chart on report page 16; AICONTROL1 on topline page 4
source_figure.filename_note: The source image filename contains 2024, but its printed fieldwork is June 9-15, 2025.

chart.rendering_note: Preserve the published 13/30/57 grouping, or use the five exact substantive categories. Do not combine this distribution with wanting more control.

separate_question_context.question_description: Comfort with the amount of control over how AI is used, versus wanting more control.
separate_question_context.rendering_note: Context or a distinct panel only. 61% wanting more control is not the complement of 57% reporting little or no control.

historical_context_only.note: 2024 values are reproduced in the 2025 topline; do not assign the 2025 sample size or margin of error to 2024. No significance claim is supplied.

indicators.what_it_shows: In June 2025, 57% of U.S. adults felt they had little or no control over AI's use in their lives.
flags: Perceived personal control, not measured political influence or actual decision authority.
Rounded percentages: the five substantive categories total 100, while adding the published 1% no-answer category yields 101. Do not normalize or silently edit values.
Pew's published grouped chart omits nonresponse; include that note.
The full-sample margin of error is a survey summary, not a category-specific confidence interval.
Separate question: desire for more control must not be stacked with felt control.
This is a 2025 observation, not a claim that no newer survey exists.
indicators.recommendation: Use the published three-part felt-control chart; retain the full topline categories for detail.

related_evidence.title: Disempowerment potential in Claude.ai conversations
related_evidence.population: Random sample of 1,499,397 Claude.ai consumer interactions; 110,233 screened in for detailed classification.
related_evidence.denominator_note: Prevalence is among sampled interactions, not only screened-in conversations, and not a percentage of users.

source_figure.locator: Figure 2, section 4.2; exact sample counts in appendix C.1
source_figure.note: Paper figure uses Wilson 95% confidence intervals. No unverified interval endpoints or digitized bar heights supplied.

related_evidence.what_it_shows: Classifier-identified potential for compromised judgment in a small fraction of sampled consumer conversations.
flags: Potential harm, not confirmed harm or demonstrated loss of agency.
Provider study of one platform; automated, partly subjective classification validated against human labels.
Categories can overlap; do not sum the three rates.
The separate historical trend uses voluntarily submitted feedback conversations and cannot establish a population trend or cause.
This measure does not capture structural political or economic disempowerment.
related_evidence.recommendation: Keep as supporting behavioral evidence, distinct from Pew's perceived-control measure.

sources.locator: Page 4, AICONTROL1 and AICONTROL2; page 1, rounding note
